title: The Shift from Chatbots to Long-Horizon Agents

questions.question: A workflow has many sequential steps that each succeed with probability 0.99, independently. What happens to its chance of full completion as steps accumulate?
options: It equals the average of the step probabilities
It falls because every step must succeed
It stays fixed because each step is reliable
It rises because later steps correct earlier ones
questions.explanation: For independent sequential steps, full success requires every step to succeed, so probabilities multiply: 0.99^n. Averaging ignores each added failure opportunity; a highly reliable step does not make the whole trajectory equally reliable.

questions.question: METR defines a model's time horizon using what point on the task-success curve?
options: The expert task duration where fitted success reaches 50 percent
The average length of all prompts in the benchmark
The duration where every model has identical accuracy
The longest task that the model completed once
questions.explanation: METR fits task success against log expert-completion time and defines the horizon where that fitted curve crosses 50%. One unusually long successful task is a single observation, not the reliability crossing.

questions.question: Assume independent per-step success of 0.99 for 70 required steps. About what is the end-to-end success probability?
options: About 99 percent, because each step has that success rate
About 49.5 percent, using 0.99 raised to the 70th power
About 70 percent, using the number of required steps
About 0.7 percent, using 0.99 divided by the step count
questions.explanation: Independent success compounds as 0.99^70≈0.495, about 49.5%, because all 70 steps must work. The 99% option mistakes per-step reliability for full-run reliability; dividing by 70 is not the probability rule.

questions.question: A model behaves more safely in a visible benchmark than during deployment. What does the lesson say about the benchmark horizon?
options: Treat it as an upper bound and evaluate the deployment distribution
Treat it as a guarantee for every production workload
Ignore it because task duration has no bearing on reliability
Treat it as a lower bound because benchmarks are harder
questions.explanation: Treat the measured horizon as an idealized ceiling and test your deployment distribution: tools, consequences, and user inputs differ from the benchmark. A guarantee for every workload overreads a 50%-success statistic.

questions.question: A proposed agent task emits hundreds of thousands of observations over a long run. What design change addresses the context problem described in the lesson?
options: Keep every raw event in the active prompt forever
Compress history and use checkpoints plus memory tiers
Review only the final answer after the agent finishes
Remove all observation logs to save tokens
questions.explanation: Raw observations and tool outputs accumulate beyond one context, so compress older history and preserve durable checkpoints and memory tiers. Keeping every event active recreates overflow; deleting all logs also erases the audit trail.

questions.question: A benchmark reports a long task horizon, but the task has irreversible customer-facing actions. What is the sound deployment decision?
options: Run task-specific evaluations and add budgets, checkpoints, and review gates
Remove safeguards so deployment conditions match the benchmark
Deploy directly because the benchmark already measured a long horizon
Replace the benchmark with a single successful demo run
questions.explanation: A benchmark measures capability under its test setup, not safe reliability for irreversible customer actions. Evaluate representative deployment tasks and bound exposure with budgets, checkpoints, and review gates; a demo success cannot establish those controls.
